data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001 frames the 'if and only if' of panel superiority as turning on conditional independence of panel-member errors given the checklist's features. But this criterion is not identifiable within a single evaluation. The target asks the evaluation to distinguish 'genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance that happens to track the right answer,' yet its proposed diagnostic—measuring whether errors cluster on non-checklisted cases—cannot separate two indistinguishable outcomes: (a) errors are conditionally independent given checklist features but the checklist is incomplete, producing clustered failures via shared feature omission, and (b) errors are correlated through shared training on the checklist, producing the same clustered failures. Both yield identical within-panel agreement patterns on incorrect items. The biconditional claim ('if and only if') thus overstates what a single evaluation can establish: it can detect error clustering, but cannot adjudicate whether the clustering stems from feature-space incompleteness (a coverage problem) or from training-induced correlation (an independence problem), which the target itself identifies as a distinct mechanism. The covering principle the target seeks—conditional independence—is not observable from the data a single evaluation provides.
